title: Myanmar
hookLine: monks marched for their people; some monks have also spread hatred, and others have opposed them

lines: WE WILL NOT ACCEPT YOUR OFFERINGS.
cards: Rows of monks in deep red robes walk through the streets of Yangon in the rain. They aren't shouting. Some are chanting the discourse on loving-kindness.
And some carry their alms bowls upside down. On the news it looks like a protest sign. To people who know the monastic rules, it's older and precise: we will not accept your offerings.

The monks were refusing gifts from the generals who ruled the country, at a time of hardship for ordinary people. Where giving to monks is part of daily life, that refusal said a great deal without words.

teach.h: THE UPTURNED BOWL, FROM THE VINAYA.
teach.b: The upturned bowl comes from the Vinaya.

In the Cullavagga, a layman falsely accuses a respected monk, and the Buddha allows the sangha to turn the bowl down toward him: the monks won't visit his house or accept his food until he makes amends.
It's a formal act, meant to be reversed when the person changes.

So when monks in Myanmar turned their bowls down to the generals, they were using an ancient rule as a nonviolent strike. The marches were met with force; monks were beaten and arrested, and monasteries were raided.
That's one face of the robe in modern Myanmar. Here's another, and it's hard.

In the years since, some monks have preached against Muslims, including the Rohingya, spreading fear and hatred in sermons and online, while violence against Rohingya communities drove families from their homes.
Those monks wore the same robe. And a third face. Other monks have spoken out against that hatred, sheltered Muslim neighbors during riots, and joined interfaith efforts, sometimes at real risk.
The Dhammapada says, in Max Muller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good."
This week ran from the last of the teachers into hard history: the lamp carried, a community made of people, kings, persecutions, a war blessed then apologized for, monks for war and for peace.
And now the same robe, used to refuse tyranny, to spread hatred, to shelter neighbors. Today's line holds on to the faces that refuse and shelter: the robe for peace.

how: In Myanmar, giving food and gifts to monks is part of daily life for Buddhists, and the overturned bowl is a formal Vinaya act; monks and lay Buddhists there and abroad remain divided on nationalism, and some lead interfaith work for peace.

games.q: you're a monk. the rulers are hurting your people, and the only gift you have to give or withhold is your bowl. what do you do?
o: turn your bowl over and refuse their gifts.
games.why: monks turned their bowls over, using an ancient Vinaya act as a nonviolent refusal of the generals' offerings.

practice: Remember the last time you heard someone speak with contempt about a group of people, a joke, a post, a comment at dinner, maybe your own, and without punishing yourself or them, notice what it does in the body.
Then picture answering it calmly with one sentence, the way a monk turns a bowl over: no shouting, just a clear refusal. Rehearse that sentence in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Myanmar. Where monks turned their bowls over to refuse the generals, where some spread hatred, and others stood against it.

orig.note: Pali patta: the alms bowl; overturning it (patta-nikkujjana) is a formal act of refusal.

carryVoice: Your line: the robe for peace. An upturned bowl can refuse without a single shout. Same time tomorrow.
